abstract: Background: Sex differences in alcohol use disorder (AUD) suggest that the neural circuits regulating alcohol intake may differ between males and females. We examined whether infralimbic neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens shell (IL-NAcSh) regulate alcohol self-administration and anxiety-related behavior following chronic intermittent alcohol (CIA) exposure. Methods: Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats were trained to self-administer 10% alcohol before receiving excitatory, inhibitory or control designer receptors exclusively activated by designer drugs (DREADDs) in NAcSh-projecting IL neurons. Rats then underwent six weeks of CIA vapor or room air exposure. Alcohol self-administration and elevated plus maze behavior was then assessed after deschloroclozapine pretreatment. Results: During acute withdrawal, IL-NAcSh inhibition increased alcohol intake in CIA-exposed males, while excitation increased intake in room air control males. Neither manipulation detectably altered alcohol intake in females. In the elevated plus maze, excitation reduced open-arm time and increased closed-arm time in males, while both excitation and inhibition reduced open-arm time in females. Conclusions: Activity in NAcSh-projecting IL neurons appears to constrain alcohol intake during acute withdrawal in CIA-exposed males. Increasing activity in these neurons did not reduce intake in this group. The divergent effects on EPM behavior and drinking suggest that this pathway's contributions to anxiety-like behavior and alcohol self-administration are partly dissociable. The absence of detectable effects on drinking in females highlights the need to identify additional pathways that regulate dependence-related alcohol use in females. Better defining the circuits that regulate withdrawal-induced drinking in males and females may guide the development of more effective, sex-informed circuit-based therapies for AUD.
